cmo-cmo-2003-01.title: Solve a congruence
cmo-cmo-2003-01.body:
After $m$ minutes the minute hand has turned $6m$ degrees and the hour hand $\frac m2$ degrees (one turn in $720$ minutes). The angle between them is $1^\circ$ exactly when
$$6m - \frac m2 = \frac{11m}{2} \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{360} \iff 11m \equiv \pm 2 \pmod{720}.$$
Since $11\cdot 131 = 1441 = 2\cdot 720 + 1$, the inverse of $11$ mod $720$ is $131$, so
$$m \equiv \pm 2\cdot 131 = \pm 262 \pmod{720}.$$
In $1 \le m \le 720$ this gives $m = 262$ and $m = 720 - 262 = 458$.

Check: $11\cdot 262 = 2882 = 4\cdot 720 + 2$ and $11\cdot 458 = 5038 = 7\cdot 720 - 2$. (At 4:22 the hands are $1^\circ$ apart, and at 7:38 likewise.)

**Answer: $m = 262$ and $m = 458$**

cmo-cmo-2003-01.title: Count multiples of 11
cmo-cmo-2003-01.body:
From $11m = 720k \pm 2$ we need $720k \pm 2 \equiv 0 \pmod{11}$. As $720 = 65\cdot 11 + 5$, this is $5k \pm 2 \equiv 0 \pmod{11}$. With $1 \le m \le 720$ we have $1 \le k \le 11$ (and $k = 11$ only with $-2$, giving $m = 719.8\ldots$, not an integer). Testing: $5k + 2 \equiv 0$ gives $k = 4$ ($22$), and $5k - 2 \equiv 0$ gives $k = 7$ ($33$). Then $m = \frac{720\cdot 4 + 2}{11} = 262$ and $m = \frac{720\cdot 7 - 2}{11} = 458$.

**Answer: $262, 458$**

cmo-cmo-2003-02.title: Binomial theorem for powers of 9
cmo-cmo-2003-02.body:
$3^{2j} = 9^j = (10 - 1)^j \equiv (-1)^j\left(1 - 10j + 100\binom j2\right) \pmod{1000}$, since higher terms contain $10^3$. For $j = 50$: $9^{50} \equiv 1 - 500 + 100\cdot 1225 = 122001 \equiv 1$, so $3^{100} \equiv 1$; for $j = 26$: $9^{26} \equiv 1 - 260 + 100\cdot 325 = 32241 \equiv 241$. With $E \equiv 52 \pmod{100}$ as in the first approach, $2003^E \equiv 3^{52} = 9^{26} \equiv 241 \pmod{1000}$.

**Answer: $241$**

cmo-cmo-2003-03.title: Some variable is less than 1
cmo-cmo-2003-03.body:
Write the first equation as $(x^3 - x) + (y^3 - y) + (z^3 - z) = 0$. If $x, y, z \ge 1$, each bracket $t^3 - t = t(t^2 - 1)$ is $\ge 0$, so all are $0$ and $x = y = z = 1$ — but then $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 3 \ne 1 = xyz$. So in any positive solution some variable is less than $1$; by symmetry say $x < 1$. Then
$$x^2 + y^2 + z^2 > y^2 + z^2 \ge 2yz > yz > xyz,$$
contradicting the second equation. So there are **no** positive real solutions.

**Answer: none**

cmo-cmo-2003-03.title: Discriminant: every variable is at least 2
cmo-cmo-2003-03.body:
Suppose a positive solution exists. Viewed as a quadratic in $x$, the second equation $x^2 - (yz)x + (y^2 + z^2) = 0$ has a real root, so its discriminant is non-negative:
$$y^2z^2 - 4y^2 - 4z^2 \ge 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac14 \ge \frac1{z^2} + \frac1{y^2} > \frac1{y^2}$$
(dividing by $4y^2z^2$). So $y > 2$; by symmetry $x, y, z > 2$. But then $x(x^2 - 1) + y(y^2 - 1) + z(z^2 - 1) > 0$, contradicting the first equation. No solutions.

**Answer: none**

cmo-cmo-2003-04.title: Positions along the line are linear in the centres
cmo-cmo-2003-04.body:
**Set-up.** Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$ and $\mathbf v$ a unit vector perpendicular to $AB$. A circle through $A$ and $B$ has its centre on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, so the centres are $O_i = M + h_i\mathbf v$ ($i = 1, 2, 3$), with $h_1, h_2, h_3$ distinct (distinct circles through $A$ and $B$ have distinct centres).

Let $\ell$ be a line through $A$ other than $AB$, with unit direction vector $\mathbf u$; then $\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v \ne 0$. Describe points of $\ell$ by their signed position $s$: the point $A + s\mathbf u$.

**Second intersections.** $A + s\mathbf u$ lies on circle $i$ iff $|A + s\mathbf u - O_i|^2 = |A - O_i|^2$, i.e. $s^2 - 2s\,\mathbf u\cdot(O_i - A) = 0$. Besides $s = 0$ (the point $A$), the root is
$$s_i = 2\,\mathbf u\cdot(O_i - A) = 2\,\mathbf u\cdot(M - A) + 2(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v)\,h_i = \lambda + \mu h_i,$$
with $\lambda$, $\mu = 2\,\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v \ne 0$ depending only on $\ell$. (If $\ell$ is tangent to circle $i$ at $A$, then $s_i = 0$ and the "intersection point" is $A$ itself; the formula still applies.) So $X$, $Y$, $Z$ are at positions $s_1$, $s_2$, $s_3$ for the circles they lie on.

**The ratio.**
$$XY = |s_2 - s_1| = |\mu|\,|h_2 - h_1|, \qquad YZ = |s_3 - s_2| = |\mu|\,|h_3 - h_2|,$$
so
$$XY : YZ = |h_2 - h_1| : |h_3 - h_2| = O_1O_2 : O_2O_3,$$
which does not depend on $\ell$. Moreover, $s_2$ lies between $s_1$ and $s_3$ exactly when $h_2$ lies between $h_1$ and $h_3$ — also independent of $\ell$ — so the labelling "$Y$ between $X$ and $Z$" assigns the same circle to $Y$ for every line. ∎

cmo-cmo-2003-04.title: Similar triangles
cmo-cmo-2003-04.body: Join $B$ to $X$, $Y$, $Z$. For every line $\ell$ through $A$, the angles $\angle AXB$, $\angle AYB$, $\angle AZB$ are inscribed angles on the chord $AB$ in the three circles, so each is constant (or replaced by its supplement when the point moves to the other arc). In the configuration of the figure ($X$, $Y$, $Z$ on the same side of $A$), triangle $BXY$ has angles $\angle BXY = 180^\circ - \angle AXB$ and $\angle BYX = \angle AYB$, and triangle $BYZ$ has $\angle BYZ = 180^\circ - \angle AYB$ and $\angle BZY = \angle AZB$; all are fixed. So for any two lines the triangles $BXY$ are similar, as are the triangles $BYZ$, and $\frac{XY}{BY}$, $\frac{YZ}{BY}$ are fixed, hence so is $XY : YZ$. When some of the points move to the other side of $A$, the same angles reappear as supplements and the argument goes through; the first approach handles all positions at once. ∎

cmo-cmo-2003-05.title: Greedy choice from the top
cmo-cmo-2003-05.body:
**The procedure.** Choose coordinates in the plane. Repeat until $S$ is used up: pick a remaining point $P$ with the largest $y$-coordinate, put $P$ into $T$, and delete from the remaining points $P$ itself and all points at distance less than $\sqrt3$ from $P$.

Any point chosen later was not deleted, so it is at distance $\ge \sqrt3$ from every earlier chosen point: any two points of $T$ are at least $\sqrt3$ apart. If each step deletes at most $7$ points, then $n \le 7|T|$, i.e. $|T| \ge n/7$. So it suffices to show: **at each step at most $6$ points other than $P$ are deleted.**

**Where the deleted points lie.** Put $P$ at the origin and use polar coordinates $(\rho, \varphi)$. A deleted point $Q \ne P$ has $1 \le \rho < \sqrt3$ (points of $S$ are at least $1$ apart) and $y_Q \le y_P$, i.e. $\varphi \in [180^\circ, 360^\circ]$. Split this half-annulus into six sectors
$$R_j = \{1 \le \rho < \sqrt3,\ 180^\circ + 30^\circ(j-1) \le \varphi \le 180^\circ + 30^\circ j\}, \quad j = 1, \ldots, 6.$$
Every deleted point lies in some $R_j$.

**Each sector has diameter less than $1$.** Take two points of one sector, $(\rho_1, \varphi_1)$ and $(\rho_2, \varphi_2)$, with $|\varphi_1 - \varphi_2| \le 30^\circ$. By the law of cosines their squared distance is
$$\rho_1^2 + \rho_2^2 - 2\rho_1\rho_2\cos(\varphi_1 - \varphi_2) \le g(\rho_1, \rho_2) := \rho_1^2 + \rho_2^2 - \sqrt3\,\rho_1\rho_2.$$
We show $g < 1$ for $\rho_1, \rho_2 \in [1, \sqrt3)$. For fixed $\rho_2$, $g$ is a strictly convex quadratic in $\rho_1$, so on $[1, \sqrt3)$ it is less than $\max\big(g(1, \rho_2), g(\sqrt3, \rho_2)\big)$, except at $\rho_1 = 1$ where it equals $g(1, \rho_2)$. Now
$$g(1, \rho_2) = 1 + \rho_2(\rho_2 - \sqrt3) < 1, \qquad g(\sqrt3, \rho_2) = 1 + (\rho_2 - 1)(\rho_2 - 2) \le 1$$
for $1 \le \rho_2 < \sqrt3$. Hence $g(\rho_1, \rho_2) < 1$ in all cases, and any two points of the same sector are less than $1$ apart.

So each sector contains at most one point of $S$, at most $6$ points besides $P$ are deleted, and each step deletes at most $7$ points. Therefore $|T| \ge n/7$. ∎
